title: Passkeys Explained: How Passwordless Login Stops Phishing (and What It Can't Fix) | FLOWMINUTE LAB
description:
Passkeys explained simply, with original animated diagrams: public vs private keys, device biometric/PIN approval, website domain binding, phishing resistance, synced vs device-bound credentials, lost-phone recovery and security tradeoffs. This is an educational illustration, not a login to any real account.

Primary sources:
FIDO Alliance: https://fidoalliance.org/passkeys/
Google developers: https://developers.google.com/identity/passkeys
NIST syncable authenticators: https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b/syncable/
Google Account recovery guidance: https://support.google.com/accounts/answer/13548313

#Passkeys #CyberSecurity #Passwordless #PhishingProtection #TechExplained

captions.text: Signing in with your fingerprint can feel like magic.
No password typed, yet the website knows it's you.
So how do passkeys actually work, and why are they harder to phish?
A passkey uses public-key cryptography instead of a reusable secret that you type.
Your device creates a key pair for the genuine website: a public key that the site can store, and a private key that stays protected on your device or in your passkey manager.
When you sign in, the site sends a fresh challenge.
Your device asks you to approve using its screen lock, fingerprint, face unlock, or PIN, then signs that challenge with the private key.
The website checks the signature using your public key.
Importantly, your fingerprint is checked locally: the website never receives your fingerprint or your private key.
Now imagine a fake sign-in page with a nearly identical address.
A passkey registered for the real domain cannot be used to authenticate on that imitation domain, because the browser and operating system bind it to the correct website.
This is what phishing-resistant means here.
It does not mean that every possible attack on an account becomes impossible.
Some passkeys are synced in encrypted form across a user's devices.
Others are bound to a physical security key or a particular device.
Syncing can help if you upgrade your phone, but the security of your account and the recovery process still matter.
NIST warns that cloud syncing and recovery introduce their own risks that services need to manage.
What happens if your phone is lost?
Depending on the account and provider, you may use a second trusted device, another passkey, a hardware security key, or the service's account recovery flow.
Google also notes that adding a passkey does not necessarily remove the old password or recovery options.
Weak fallback methods can remain a path for attackers.
Here's your practical setup checklist.
First, add a passkey to a trusted account that supports it and protect your devices with a strong screen lock.
Second, keep a secure backup sign-in or recovery option, and review the account's list of passkeys after losing a device.
Third, use the passkey prompt only when you started the sign-in yourself, and read unusual requests before approving.
So remember the difference: passwords are reusable strings you can accidentally give away.
Passkeys prove control of a protected key for a specific website, without revealing that key.
Phishing resistance is a major improvement, not a promise of perfect security.
Check your recovery methods, secure your devices, and use passkeys where available.
